title: Drafted into the Army band in France, learning trombone
summary: Drafted and sent to France, he talked his way into the band, learned trombone with help from Willie Foster, and played for troops for 18 months.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Where were you? In France.
In France. I was in, in Bush, France. Bush. Yeah.
Did you join the, that was pretty early, wasn't it? Were you drafted or did you?

No, they drafted. They drafted. Yeah. Yeah. So how did they come pick up trombone? Which the lieutenant was, he wanted the band, you know, for the company. And so he asked them, any fellas had an idea they wanted to take apart in music. Well I knew I could play guitar, but I didn't put no trombone. So they had a fellas from Paulianville, or Onis Heims, he's from Boerleg, he's played in the Claiborne Williams band, well they were a good musician. Willie Foster, well he was from here, and he was a good musician. So he told me, I said, Willie, he called me Bob, he said, I said, I'm a good musician.

Bob said, man, come on, we'll take a tram on. We learn you how to play. I said, oh man, I don't want to fool nothing like that. He said, man, you see who done took the raffles from us? He said, no, I said, listen, you got to shovel, you got to pick. You got to handle both them things. You got to dig a hole and shovel all that, that, that. I said, man, that's true, too. He said, look, every day. And we had them big heavy shoes on, and that again, them fellas was in the band, nice, them nice Army Ruskin shoes, you know, light shoes, keep them shining, nice leg. I said, oh, I'm going to get on this stuff myself.
They didn't have to work hard then, huh?
No, just go to the YMC and this every day in rehearsal. So in that morning when they called the roll, understand, I stepped on up, I just took a chance.
I took a chance, man, walk up there.

Lieutenant, Fire Lieutenant, they named Lieutenant Lyons, too. I said, all right, Robson, you want to play trombone? I said, yes, sir. I said, all right. I said, well, give me a brand new chord on trombone. So I just took it and put it together, you know. But I could pull it up, understand? Well, every day, so after, they had a fella who was working with the band, but it was three or four weeks, and he couldn't even pull his horn up. You know, and I just, every day, I just would take him, and after rehearsal, I would take him down behind the hill, you know, and show him how to handle his position, you see, you know what I mean? So after that, so I just take me and him both, you know.
Yeah.

Every day after that, you know, behind the hills and feet together, have the trombone, and I just have his hand and show him how to put the position. And after that, I said, but two weeks time, I thought I'd run my scales, you know. And this fella, he couldn't blow nothing.
Did Willie Foster help you much?

Yeah, Willie Foster, yeah. Willie had to lead the violin, had his violin, and every day, when I get a chance, you know, I'd go by Willie with his violin, he'd play a song for me, and I'd take the trombone, it was vamp, you know, he'd show him what to make with this vamp. And then I got to doing that, and so everything went on fine. So the other time I played, he wasn't doing nothing so much, and so they had us both in the band together, you know, playing in a jazz band. Yeah. But he just confused because he couldn't play that by making all the chords. So Lieutenant Lyons said, well, I think the best, we got to put this fella back in the big band and let Jim play by himself, you understand, in the small band. Yeah, in the small band. And man, after that, I went on, after that, yeah. Like to me, that thing just come to me overnight. I swear to Christ, that trombone, come to me overnight. You know, my whole heart and mind had got hurt. And like this come to me, this overnight. And man, we went out there, and three weeks time, man, we gone all over France, playing for the lieutenants, for the buck private. The buck private treat you better than lieutenants there, because you get more money from the buck private. Just boil the liquor you want and different stuff. And the lieutenants, sometimes they'll give you a good pay, sometimes they'll give you nothing. Yeah, man, that's, I went out a lot, I see a lot of friends.
Anybody else in that band that you remember from New Orleans? Just Willie Foster, anybody else? Willie Foster, let me see.
Willie had a bunch of fellas from New Orleans, but he wasn't playing in the band, you know. Yeah. Those fellas was overseas with me, you know. I wasn't in the band, though.
No, they wasn't in the band.
I meet the Latin fellas right now, and I go downtown. All the way around, back, St. Bernard Street. Yeah. I made a bunch of them. It's the last time I was down there for the meeting.
Did you stay in France until the war was all over then?
No, man, I stayed in France, say, but, to France 18 months. 18 months. 18 months. 18 months. I took so long, I hadn't thought he was going to send me back home.
Did you learn any French over there? I couldn't say nothing.

I'll tell you one thing, but then people, I got rid of it with my American money, because you see, I couldn't count their money, so I'd give them my American dollar, and so they used to give me any kind of change of that money, you understand? I didn't know what it was, but they liked that American dollar. Well, because they'd run you down for American dollar.
